description: 20 new formulations annotated against the familiar saved corpus before first execution. Not a new-document benchmark. Multiple-evidence questions may use multiple facts in one passage; ordinary Hit@k measures any annotated evidence, not complete coverage.

questions.question: Which three main types of diabetes does the overview list?

evidence.quote: There are three main types of diabetes: type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes

questions.expected_behavior: Name type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes.

questions.question: According to the article, where should someone follow up after a blood sugar test at a health fair?

evidence.quote: follow up at a clinic or doctor's office to make sure the results are accurate.

questions.expected_behavior: At a clinic or doctor’s office to ensure accuracy.

questions.question: How does the article describe blood sugar levels in prediabetes?

evidence.quote: blood sugar levels are higher than normal, but not high enough for a type 2 diabetes diagnosis.

questions.expected_behavior: Higher than normal but not high enough for a type 2 diagnosis.

questions.question: What pregnancy weeks do the documents give for gestational diabetes testing?

evidence.quote: between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy

questions.expected_behavior: Report 24–28 weeks as the document’s guidance, not personalized advice.

questions.question: According to this document snapshot, approximately what percentage of diagnosed diabetes cases are type 2?

evidence.quote: Type 2 diabetes accounts for about 90% to 95% of all diagnosed cases of diabetes

questions.expected_behavior: About 90%–95%; preserve approximation and snapshot framing.

questions.question: Do the documents mention cuts taking ages to heal as a type 2 symptom?

evidence.quote: Cuts, sores, or wounds that are very slow to heal.

questions.expected_behavior: Yes, cuts/sores/wounds slow to heal; no diagnosis.

questions.question: Where does the article say darker skin patches might appear?

evidence.quote: Dark patches of skin around the neck, armpits, or groin.

questions.expected_behavior: Neck, armpits or groin.

questions.question: Does the symptoms page list pins and needles in hands or feet?

evidence.quote: Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet.

questions.expected_behavior: Yes, numbness or tingling in hands or feet.

questions.question: Does gestashonal diabetes usually go away after the baby is born?

evidence.quote: Gestational diabetes usually goes away after your baby is born.

questions.expected_behavior: Usually goes away; do not state always.

questions.question: Which diabetes type is linked to the body attacking itself by mistake?

evidence.quote: Type 1 diabetes is thought to be caused by an autoimmune reaction

questions.expected_behavior: Type 1; preserve thought-to-be qualification.

questions.question: How do the documents contrast insulin production in type 1 with insulin use in type 2?

evidence.quote: This reaction stops your body from making insulin.
With type 2 diabetes, your body doesn’t use insulin well

questions.expected_behavior: Explain type 1 stops insulin production and type 2 does not use insulin well; cite each.

questions.question: What do the documents say about gestational diabetes after birth and the mother’s later type 2 risk?

evidence.quote: Gestational diabetes usually goes away after your baby is born.
it increases your risk for type 2 diabetes later in life.

questions.expected_behavior: Usually goes away after birth but raises later type 2 risk.

questions.question: Do the articles give the same prevention guidance for type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

evidence.quote: Currently, no one knows how to prevent type 1 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes can be prevented or delayed with lifestyle changes.

questions.expected_behavior: Distinguish no known type 1 prevention from lifestyle prevention/delay for type 2.

questions.question: According to the type 2 article, do medicines replace healthy eating and activity, and who should advise on blood sugar targets?

evidence.quote: You'll still need to eat healthy and be active if you take insulin or other medicines.
Ask your doctor how often to check your blood sugar and what your target blood sugar levels should be.

questions.expected_behavior: Medicines do not replace healthy eating/activity; ask doctor about targets.

questions.question: Why does the symptoms article describe gestational testing even when symptoms are absent, and what timing does it give?

evidence.quote: Gestational diabetes doesn’t usually have symptoms.
between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy

questions.expected_behavior: Usually no symptoms; testing between weeks 24–28. Avoid inventing a diagnostic mechanism.

questions.question: What exact HbA1c percentage diagnoses diabetes according to these documents?
questions.expected_behavior: insufficient_evidence; numeric HbA1c cutoff absent.

questions.question: What exact daily metformin dose do these articles recommend?
questions.expected_behavior: insufficient_evidence; no dosing given.

questions.question: What email address does the article give for a diabetes educator?
questions.expected_behavior: insufficient_evidence; do not invent contact details.

questions.question: Why does gestational diabetes always cause obvious symptoms, according to the documents?

evidence.quote: Gestational diabetes doesn’t usually have symptoms.

questions.expected_behavior: Correct false premise: it usually does not have symptoms; do not accept always.

questions.question: Which guaranteed cure for diabetes do these documents describe?

evidence.quote: There isn't a cure yet for diabetes

questions.expected_behavior: Reject premise: document says no cure yet; do not label lifestyle changes a guaranteed cure.
